seats.name: seat-1
argv:
Read spec.txt (the STAMP language) and program.stamp. Determine exactly what the program outputs
when run under that specification.

Write your final answer, and only your final answer with no explanation, to a file named
answer.txt in your current working directory: the printed values in order, separated by single
spaces, on one line.

The room's final agreed proposal text must be exactly your answer and nothing else (no explanation) — that text is read as the submitted answer once the room concludes.

Join room rq1 as seat-1 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room reached consensus (3/3 agree) on the program's output, and I've written it to `answer.txt`. I checked it by hand-tracing the program. I didn't run it, because there's no STAMP interpreter here.

```
12 1 9 0 0 12 3 45 6 3007 3005 3008 41 40 104 99 104 24 9 11 11 10 479001600 45 8 19 7 0 77 0 0 15 15 16 15 255 1099511627776 3
```

My first trace gave `1027 1008` for the `outer`/`mid` prints. The other two seats had `3007 3005`, and they were right. Scope is per call, so `deep` sees only its own `c`. It reads `a` and `b` as the globals 1000 and 2000, not the values from its callers' frames.

I've left the room.

argv:

The room's final agreed proposal text must be exactly your answer and nothing else (no explanation) — that text is read as the submitted answer once the room concludes.

Join room rq1 as seat-2 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room agreed on this output (proposal `prop_90ed1609`, all three seats voted agree), and it is in `answer.txt`:

`12 1 9 0 0 12 3 45 6 3007 3005 3008 41 40 104 99 104 24 9 11 11 10 479001600 45 8 19 7 0 77 0 0 15 15 16 15 255 1099511627776 3`

I got this by tracing the program by hand against `spec.txt`, not by running it. The only disagreement was seat-1's opening answer, which had `1027 1008` where the rest of us had `3007 3005`. That answer treated the nested procedures as closures over their caller's locals. The spec's SCOPE section says a call reads only its own locals, then globals. So `deep` sees the globals `a`=1000 and `b`=2000, and seat-1 then agreed.

Someone overwrote `answer.txt` with seat-1's version partway through. I confirmed the file now holds the agreed line. I have left the room.

seats.text:
The room reached 3/3 consensus on the program's output, and I've left it. `answer.txt` holds the agreed line:

`12 1 9 0 0 12 3 45 6 3007 3005 3008 41 40 104 99 104 24 9 11 11 10 479001600 45 8 19 7 0 77 0 0 15 15 16 15 255 1099511627776 3`

This is a hand trace of the program against the spec, not something I ran. seat-1 first had `1027 1008` where the agreed line has `3007 3005`. seat-1 had read the `outer` and `mid` locals from inside `deep`. The spec's scope is per call, so `deep` reads globals `a` = 1000 and `b` = 2000. seat-1 then adopted the same answer.

The hub required a verify entry from someone other than the proposer before the proposal could pass. My own `verify/seat-3` entry was refused because the room had already concluded. seat-2's entry, and seat-1's, were enough for the vote to pass.
